content.intro: Learn row-level and fine-grained security through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Row-Level and Fine-Grained Security matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: Row-Level and Fine-Grained Security
content_blocks.alt_text: A row-level security policy compares each row's tenant ID with the current session's allowed tenant and filters other rows.
content_blocks.caption: Row-level security adds a database-enforced row predicate; role, ownership, and setting controls still require testing.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The goal of row-level and fine-grained security is to reduce what identities and queries are allowed to do. Apply defense in depth: parameterize values, grant least privilege, protect sensitive data, and verify denial cases as well as allowed cases.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Row-level security concepts, Row access policies, Tenant data isolation, Policy testing. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Row-level security concepts
items.text: Row-level security concepts should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

items.title: Row access policies
items.text: Row access policies helps you apply least privilege, safe parameterized access, sensitive-data protection, auditing, and database-level isolation controls. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Tenant data isolation
items.text: Tenant data isolation is about keeping multi-step work correct when errors or other sessions intervene. Keep transactions short, define what must succeed together, handle conflicts explicitly, and test using separate sessions in a disposable database.

items.title: Policy testing
items.text: Policy testing makes SQL easier to change safely. Turn assumptions into repeatable checks, keep schema/query changes reviewable, use deterministic ordering, and record the data shape and environment used for the check.

items.title: Limits of relying solely on application-side filters
items.text: Limits of relying solely on application-side filters makes SQL easier to change safely. Turn assumptions into repeatable checks, keep schema/query changes reviewable, use deterministic ordering, and record the data shape and environment used for the check.

content_blocks.expected_output: The policy compares each row's tenant_id with a session setting and applies both read filtering and write checks. This is a teaching sketch: real applications must set the value securely, test roles/ownership, and prevent users from changing it arbitrarily.

The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Row-Level and Fine-Grained Security is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
